bib.title: Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool", Rajesh Jayaram (first author), Drew Tyler, David Woodruff, Corinna Cortes, Yossi Matias, Vahab Mirrokni, Vincent Cohen-Addad (Google Research). Preprint, arXiv 2606.28277v1 [cs.LG], 26 Jun 2026 (June 2026).

COVERAGE: 35,866 of 35,866 chars, 10 of 10 pages, including references. No appendices exist. Figure 1 is text-only in the extraction. No embedded instructions found.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The paper proposes four roles for AI in peer review, modelled on SAE vehicle autonomy levels and on Feng et al. 2026. The roles are: 1 tool for authors; 2 tool for reviewers; 3 supporting reviewer (3.5 adds ratings); 4 total automation. Human responsibility shifts from author or reviewer to area chair to nobody.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual taxonomy. It has no empirical test.
  quote: "Our taxonomy parallels both the SAE Levels of Vehicle Autonomy, as well as the levels of autonomy for mathematical research presented in [7]."
  where: p.7, section 4
- On a SPOT subset, the multi-stage PAT pipeline found 89.7% of equation and proof errors. Zero-shot Gemini 3.1 Pro found 55.2%, and the original SPOT state of the art scored 21.1%.
  number: 89.7% vs 55.2% vs 21.1%
  setup: 26 Math/CS papers with 29 "Equation / proof" errors (retracted or errata). An LLM grader judges logical equivalence, and an author audited each grade. The numbers are not comparable to the SPOT paper's strict grader.
  quote: "PAT (Gemini 3.1 Pro) 89.7%" and "Gemini 3.1 Pro [8] (Zero-Shot) 55.2%" and "Original SPOT SOTA [15] 21.1%"
  where: p.4, Table 2
  note: the abstract's "34% improvement" is the gap 89.7 minus 55.2, so it is percentage points. The text calls it a "34% gain improvement".
- Pass@k raises recall but hurts precision, so the human must sift for valid errors. PAT's architecture addresses this with four stages: a segmenter, adaptive per-segment compute budgets, Deep Review agents, and a synthesis agent. The synthesis agent deduplicates, checks severity and grounds claims with search.
  number: about 100 proposed issues per valid critical error (illustrative arithmetic, not measured)
  quote: "If a model outputs 10 potential issues per pass, and has a 10% chance of finding a critical issue per pass, running it 10 times forces a human to sift through∼100 proposed issues just to find one valid, critical error."
  where: p.3
- Pilots: PAT was given to authors only, as Role 1, once per manuscript, before submission. STOC ran in Nov 2025 and ICML in Jan 2026. More than 4,700 submissions were reviewed.
  number: over 4,700
  setup: Gemini 2.5 Deep Think for both pilots. The STOC pipeline was math-only and the ICML pipeline was generalised. Authors were not in the formal review.
  quote: "Between the two conferences, over4,700submissions were reviewed by the PAT system."
  where: p.5
- Author survey (STOC n=124, ICML n=733; self-selected respondents, no control group). The two rows below carry the main risk.
  number: grounded 55.8% and 64.8%; substantive theory gaps 11.6% and 35.4%; ran new experiments 31% (ICML); very or mostly helpful 92.7% and 90.7%
  quote: "Feedback Mostly or All Grounded55.8% 64.8%" and "Identified Substantive Theory Gaps11.6% 35.4%" and "Ran New Experiments– 31%"
  where: p.6, Table 3
  note: only about 55-65% of authors found the feedback mostly grounded, so reviews still need human verification. This supports human review.
- Peer-review human consistency is weak. In the NeurIPS 2021 experiment, 10% of submissions were routed through two committees and 23% of decisions were inconsistent. Random selection at the 22.7% acceptance rate would give 35%. The rate drops to 16% when borderline papers are excluded.
  number: 23% vs 35% random vs 16%
  quote: "routed10%of submissions through two independent review committees and found a23%inconsistency rate in acceptance decisions."
  where: p.8
  note: cited as an argument that human review is a noisy baseline for Role 4.
- Reported pilot failure modes: date hallucination and knowledge cutoffs, PDF parsing issues, and falsely declaring a correct proof wrong. The authors say they fixed the first two with search and parsing, and the third is "a product of any LLM based system".
  where: p.7
- Role risks:
  - Role 1: papers look superficially stronger, which hides issues from reviewers.
  - Role 2: reviewers verify the AI review instead of the paper, may hide their AI use and may double down on wrong AI points. The authors suggest letting authors flag hallucinated review points.
  - Role 3: hallucinations can affect decisions.
  - Role 4: less diversity of opinion, and authors may game the review agents.
  - Other concerns: reviewer deskilling and unclear lines of accountability.
  where: p.7-9
- Context figures: 21% of ICLR 2026 reviews were fully AI-generated (Pangram). Combined submissions to ICLR, ICML and NeurIPS were 17,051 in 2020 and an estimated 73,883 in 2026. The 2026 NeurIPS figure is an estimate.
  where: p.2 and p.7, Table 1

LIMITS
- The SPOT subset is tiny (26 papers, 29 errors). The grader is custom and not comparable to the original benchmark.
- Survey bias is not discussed: respondents self-selected, with no counterfactual and no false-positive rate. There is no precision number for PAT at all.
- Roles 3 to 4 are speculative, with no data. Role 2 is not tested either. Current systems are placed at Roles 1 and 2.
- Authors are Google employees evaluating Google's own tool. Not stated: the compute cost. The cited blog posts and the AAAI-26 pilot are not read.
- The pilots used Gemini 2.5 Deep Think, while the SPOT test used Gemini 3.1 Pro. The two are not the same model.

BUILDS ON: SAE vehicle autonomy levels; Feng et al. 2026 (autonomous mathematics research levels); Son et al. 2025 (SPOT); Beygelzimer et al. 2021 and Cortes & Lawrence 2021 (NeurIPS consistency experiments); Biswas et al. 2026 (AAAI-26 AI review pilot); Yang et al. 2025 (Paper Copilot).

CODE: none.

FIGURES: Fig. 1, p.4, "System architecture of PAT showing the four-stage inference scaling pipeline." It shows segmentation, adaptive budgeting (Light/Medium/High), Deep Review and Global Synthesis. It is the fastest way to explain a plan, fan-out, verify, merge shape. I did not run the figures script, and Fig. 1 appears only as text.

FIT TO NOTES
- 07 autonomy ladder fits best, but only as a side illustration. The Roles ladder is a human-role ladder (author, reviewer, area chair, none) in a non-loop domain, with a human-in-the-loop gate at each rung. It supports "each rung moves human responsibility one step", and the 11-65% grounding stats support keeping human review at the lower rungs. Cite it as an analogy and not as evidence about loops. I read only the first 25 lines of note 07 (front matter and framing) and did not check whether it already uses an SAE analogy.
- 03 scorekeeper: weak fit. PAT's synthesis stage (dedupe, severity, search grounding) is a verifier. The Pass@k precision argument is a useful note on verifier cost.
- Overall: marginal for loop engineering. It is not a loop paper. It is a single-pass multi-agent pipeline, with no iteration or stop condition. Use it for a "sharpens" citation at most.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean. The first-page "34%" is ambiguous (see the SPOT claim). The Google Search and DeepThink parts of the pipeline are not described in detail.
